name: Vocabulary Complexity
description: Evaluates the sophistication, rarity, and register of the vocabulary used throughout a document. Large Language Models are designed to maximize user comprehension and token efficiency, which inherently biases them toward a 'middle-of-the-road' vocabulary. They heavily rely on statistically probable, commonly used words and standard 'academic' phrasing (e.g., 'furthermore', 'crucial', 'delve'). While AI can use complex words, it distributes them evenly and predictably, rarely deploying truly obscure, archaic, or idiosyncratic terms unless specifically prompted. In contrast, human experts often exhibit 'spiky' vocabulary profiles—mixing highly specialized, rare jargon with colloquialisms in ways that deviate from standard statistical norms.
algorithm: Lexical Sophistication & Word Frequency Rank Profiling
mechanism: The model parses the text and evaluates every word against established massive corpus frequency lists (e.g., Subtlex, Google Web Trillion Word Corpus). It calculates a 'complexity profile' based on the ratio of high-frequency (common) words to low-frequency (rare/complex) words. Furthermore, it analyzes the semantic register of the complex words used. A text that maintains a relentlessly consistent, evenly distributed 'moderately high' vocabulary complexity (often reading like a high school or undergraduate essay) without any unpredictable spikes into extremely rare or domain-idiosyncratic terminology is a strong mathematical signature of an LLM seeking to balance eloquence with generic readability.
useCase: Crucial for analyzing academic papers, professional journalism, and creative writing. It helps differentiate between the genuine, nuanced expertise of a human author and the simulated, averaged-out 'smart' tone of an AI.
strengths:
• Highly effective at detecting the 'ChatGPT Tone'—that distinct feeling of a text being overly polished, articulate, but ultimately leaning on generic 'smart-sounding' words (like 'multifaceted', 'tapestry', 'testament').
• Difficult to bypass simply by asking the AI to 'write like an expert', as the AI's idea of expertise is still bound by predictable token probabilities.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives if analyzing human writers who intentionally write in a highly standardized, accessible language (like ESL learners or technical writers following strict plain-language guidelines).
• Less effective on very short texts where there isn't enough word volume to establish a statistical frequency baseline.
parameters:
Analysis: Corpus Frequency Matching & Register Evaluation
Metric: Mean Word Frequency Rank & Idiographic Lexical Spikes
Output: 0-100 Lexical Artificiality Score
accuracy: High — 75-85% accuracy. It is one of the most reliable semantic indicators, as LLMs struggle to organically replicate the mathematically inefficient and unbalanced vocabulary choices of true human experts.

references.title: Manning, C.D. & Schütze, H. (1999). Foundations of Statistical Natural Language Processing. MIT Press.
Biber, D. (1988). Variation across Speech and Writing. Cambridge University Press.
